title: Social Media and Mental Health: What Research Actually Shows
description: Does social media cause depression and anxiety? A nuanced look at the research, what's overblown, what's real, and practical recommendations.

content.text: Headlines scream that social media is destroying a generation. But what does the research actually show? It's more nuanced than you'd think.
A meta-analysis of 226 studies found social media use is associated with depression and anxiety, but the effect size is small (r=0.15-0.20)—comparable to eating potatoes.
For context, this means social media explains about 2-4% of the variation in mental health. Other factors matter much more.
Does social media cause depression, or do depressed people use more social media? Both are probably true, creating a feedback loop.
Several studies suggest social media's negative effects are concentrated in teenage girls, particularly around social comparison, body image, and cyberbullying.
content.citation: Twenge et al., Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 2018

content.text: Scrolling passively (comparing yourself to others) is associated with worse outcomes than active engagement (messaging friends, creating content).
The clearest harm may be indirect: social media use at night disrupts sleep, which significantly impacts mental health.

items: Social media is NOT the primary driver of teen mental health decline
Most teens use social media without significant harm
The 'phones are destroying children' narrative is too simple
Notice how specific apps make you feel
Curate your feed ruthlessly (unfollow accounts that trigger comparison)
Set time limits if use feels compulsive
Delay social media until at least 13
The relationship matters more than the rules

content.text: Social media isn't destroying mental health, but it's not harmless either. The effects are modest and vary by person. Pay attention to how specific platforms make you feel, protect your sleep, and don't let passive scrolling replace real connection.
